p.t: In short
**Add up every cost of a sale** (product, shipping, payment fees, ads, fixed costs, refunds) before you set any price.
**Keep the product cost at or below half of MAP** (the minimum advertised price, the lowest price the brand lets you show), and keep ad cost per sale at or below 10% of MAP.
**Check shipping before you list** heavy or bulky items, because freight can wipe out the profit.
**Keep ROAS above break-even.** ROAS (return on ad spend) is the sales money you earn per ad dollar. Below break-even, every sale loses money.

Set the selling price so that **70%** of the price is left after all costs of the order. This is the main target.
If 70% is not possible, **67%** is the lowest acceptable margin.
Every discount, free gift or bundle must still make a profit after product cost, shipping and ad spend.

Fill **every** cell in the calculator, even with 0, or the results show errors.
Before you list a product, check that **net profit** (money left after all costs) is above the threshold.
The full cost stack comes before any price

**Before you set a price**, list every cost for each sale and for each month.
The costs are:

The total supplier price (product plus shipping),
payment fees,
customer acquisition cost (what ads cost to win one new customer),

fixed costs (costs that stay the same each month),
a reserve for returns (money set aside for refunds).
Only then do you know two things: the break-even point (the sales level where you neither gain nor lose) and the margin each sale needs. The margin is the money left from a sale after its costs.
A price that ignores payment fees, acquisition cost, fixed costs and refunds can turn a sale that looks profitable into a loss.

**Check the full cost stack** before you trust a sticker price (the price tag shown).
**Acquisition cost matters only for paid traffic**, meaning visitors you pay ads to bring.
If most customers come through word of mouth, acquisition cost has little effect on pricing.
If you buy traffic with paid ads, every price must cover acquisition cost on top of product cost and fees.

Example: a product costs $10 from the supplier and sells for $15.
That leaves too little room to cover acquisition, fees, returns and profit.
**With paid ads, a gap that narrow is very hard to make profitable.**

**Use a profit calculator** (a tool that works out profit from your numbers) before you create any offer.
Use it to:
calculate profit margins,

set new ROAS and CPA targets (CPA is the ad cost per new customer),
check that the offer stays profitable at scale (when you sell a lot).

**Verify it stays profitable at scale.**
Reduce unit economics (the money made or lost on one order) aggressively:
product cost,

operating expenses (running costs),
fulfilment cost per order (the cost to pick, pack and ship each order).
**Every dollar saved per unit becomes budget for advertising**, which is the core lever for scaling (growing sales).

Wholesale means COGS (cost of goods sold). COGS is only the product price you pay the supplier.
**Shipping is a separate cost and is not included in wholesale.**
Profit per sale formulas

**Net profit per sale** is what you keep after all costs.
Formula: net profit per sale = MAP − COGS − ad budget per sale − shipping cost.
**Keep COGS at or below 50% of MAP**, and the ad budget per sale at or below 10% of MAP.

Profit per sale = selling price (at or above MAP) − wholesale cost − shipping cost (if shipping is free) − advertising cost per sale.
**Keep advertising cost within about 10%** of the selling price.
Profit per sale = selling price − wholesale price − shipping cost − payment processing fee (the charge the payment service takes) − advertising cost per sale.

Heavy items with high shipping costs need this check before the product is listed, because margins can be very thin.
**Check this before the product is listed.**
Profit per order = selling price − supplier wholesale cost − card processing fees (about 2.9%) − advertising cost per sale − shipping cost, if you offer free shipping.

Older advice (2021).
Net profit per sale = MAP − wholesale − average shipping cost − ad cost per sale.

Example: MAP $1,000, wholesale $500, shipping $150, ad cost $100.
**That gives $250 profit**, a 25 percent net margin.
Profit before shipping per sale = MAP − wholesale − ad spend (up to 10% of MAP) − payment fee (2.9% of MAP).

Example: MAP $1,000 and wholesale $500 leave about $371 before shipping.
That is after $100 of ad spend and a $29 fee.
Profit before ads = sale price − wholesale cost − shipping cost − Amazon fees (including the referral fee, the commission Amazon takes per sale).
Example: $19.97 − $3.00 wholesale − $1.50 shipping − $6.40 Amazon fees = **$9.07 profit before ads**.

The Amazon referral fee in this example is 15 percent of the sale price.
Net margin = (sale price − wholesale − shipping − ad cost per sale) ÷ sale price.

Example: $1,000 − $500 wholesale − $150 shipping − $100 traffic (visitors) leaves $250.
That is **25%**, below the 30% target used in this handbook.

Older advice (2019).
Break-even price for a bulky product (large and heavy) sold with free shipping:
minimum selling price = COGS + average shipping cost + other per-order costs.
Other per-order costs are customer acquisition, card processing fees, traffic and the seller's time.

If the price only equals COGS plus shipping, net profit is $0 before those other costs.
**So every sale loses money once they are added.**
Worked example at 30% off MAP with free shipping

A $600 product costs $420 from the supplier (600 × 0.70).
That leaves a $180 margin (600 − 420).

The ad budget is up to $60 (10% of MAP).
That leaves $120 (180 − 60).
**Subtract the card fee** of 2.9% of the sale and other order fees from that $120.
Older advice (2020).
Before you list a dropship product (a product your supplier ships straight to the customer, so you never hold stock),

add the supplier product price to the shipping cost for the destination country.
This total is the **landed cost** (product price plus shipping to the buyer's country).

Example: a cup washer costs $5.95 for the chosen variant (the size or style you pick).
With shipping to a US address (shipping $12.90), it totals $18.85.

Compare this with the planned selling price of $39.99.
**List the product only when the gap leaves enough room** for ads, fees and profit.

Test every product first against this baseline.
**The minimum profit margin should be at least two to three times the cost of shipping and fulfilling the item.**

Heavy and bulky items need the shipping check before listing.
Reason: freight (the cost to ship large or heavy goods) depends on size and weight, not on the selling price.

Doubling the wholesale cost is not enough on its own.
Example: an $80 product sold at 2x (price twice the wholesale cost) leaves only $80 to cover shipping, ads, fees and profit.
Older advice (2023 is not flagged; this statement is from 2023).
Example: a $180 futon (a sofa bed) with $90 wholesale and $250 freight **loses $160 per order**.
A $1,800 leather sectional (a large corner sofa) with $900 wholesale and the same $250 freight **keeps $650 per order**.
Example: a bulky home gym sells for $2,500 and the wholesale cost is $1,250, giving $1,250 gross (before shipping, fees and ads).
Landed cost and shipping (continued)

Shipping costs about $400, leaving $850.
After the order processing fee, about $800 remains.
Ads to acquire the customer cost about $100, leaving about $700 net.
The takeaway: bulky or heavy products only work when the selling price is high enough to carry the shipping costs.

**A $600 item that costs over half its price to ship is not worth selling.**
Freight and order costs for big items:

With free shipping, a $500 item costing $250 leaves $250 of margin.
A $3,000 item costing $1,500 leaves $1,500.
If free shipping costs about $300 on a large item, the cheap item drops to **about −$50, a loss**. The source printed $50, but $250 − $300 = −$50.

The expensive item keeps about $1,200.
Older advice (2021).
Shipping cost depends on distance, so orders to far-away regions can cost much more than nearby ones.

**Calculate the average shipping cost per product.** Raise prices or charge shipping where profit is too thin.
Older advice (2021-22).
Example of a thin-margin order:
A customer paid $500 for two units of the same product, with no discount, paid via PayPal (an online payment service), and no sales tax.

The supplier total was $475 ($250 for products, $225 for shipping).
The PayPal fee was $14.80 and fraud insurance (protection against fake orders) was $5.

Result: gross profit $25, net profit $5.20, net margin 1.04%.
Here shipping almost equals product cost. **That signals the price should go up or shipping should be charged.**

Older advice (2021-22).
Batch size must match product margin.
Small batches (how many units you order at once) cost more to ship per unit.
Landed cost and shipping (continued)

This is affordable only if each unit earns enough margin.
On a $400 product, small-batch shipping is a minor issue.
**On a $50 product, high shipping costs can wipe out profit.**
Example of spread versus shipping, stand-up desks. The spread is the gap between MAP and wholesale.

Average package: 5 ft × 6 in × 24 in. Average weight: 100 lb. Average shipping: $200 per order.
Older advice (2022).
**A (standard)**

MAP price: $1,000
Wholesale (50%): $500
Spread: $500
Left after $200 shipping: $300
**B (standard)**

MAP price: $1,200
Wholesale (50%): $600
Spread: $600
Left after $200 shipping: $400
**C (solid wood, premium)**

MAP price: $2,000
Wholesale (50%): $1,000
Spread: $1,000
Left after $200 shipping: $800
**D (budget)**

MAP price: $700
Wholesale (50%): $350
Spread: $350
Left after $200 shipping: $150

Spread = MAP price − wholesale cost.
Net after shipping = spread − average shipping cost per package.

**Free shipping is paid from the margin.**
Older advice (2022).
A budget desk with MAP $400 and wholesale $200 leaves a $200 spread.

After $200 average shipping, **nothing is left**.
The 2.9% transaction fee then makes the sale a loss.
Older advice (2022).

Ad costs and merchant fees (payment fees the store pays) must come out of the spread after shipping.
A remaining $150 can look fine but may not cover them.

**Check whether the product is still worth advertising before you scale it.**
Older advice (2022).
Spread between MAP and wholesale
Margin before expenses = MAP − wholesale cost.
With a MAP at 2x wholesale, a $500 wholesale cost leaves **$500** to cover ads, fees and shipping.

The starting point for profit is the spread between MAP and wholesale.
**Net profit should aim for 30%.**
The other levers (things you can change) are customer acquisition cost and shipping cost.
Profit margin is set by the spread between wholesale cost and MAP.

After negotiating supplier pricing, the biggest remaining costs are shipping and ad spend.
Older advice (2023 is not flagged).
At a selling price of 2x wholesale, gross margin = (selling price − wholesale cost) ÷ selling price.

Example: (1,000 − 500) ÷ 1,000 = **50%** before card fees, shipping and ad costs.
These remaining costs must come out of this 50% to reach a net profit of about 30%.

Margins below the 50% spread are not a standard target.
A lower margin can be acceptable only when each sale still brings in large absolute profit (many dollars per sale).

Examples: a very expensive item, or a large bulk order.
A high product price alone does not justify a low margin.

**An item priced around $4,000 with a 10% margin is still not acceptable.**
A 25% profit margin does not mean paying 75% of the sale price for the product.

After cost of goods sold, the remaining money must cover shipping, ad costs, processing fees, team costs and net profit.
Older advice (2018).

On a $1,000 sale, wholesale should be $500 or less.
That leaves about $500 for shipping, ads, fees and profit.

The minimum target in this example is **$250 net profit**, which is 25% of the sale price.
Older advice (2018).

With careful control of shipping, ads and fees, net profit margins can reach about 40%.
Margins below that depend on the same cost control.
Older advice (2018).
Doubling the wholesale cost is not enough. See the spread-and-freight case above.
Payment fees
Card processing fee of about 2.9% of the sale is used in several older worked examples.
Calculator gateway rule: the payment gateway is the service that takes the card payment.

The standard Shopify Payments example (Shopify's built-in payment service) is **5.5% of the price plus $0.30**.
Use your own Shopify Payments rate if it differs.

Worked gateway figures in the calculator:
A $40 price on site gives a gateway fee of **$2.50** (5.5% × 40 + 0.30).

An $80 price on site gives **$4.70** (5.5% × 80 + 0.30).
In the PayPal example above, the fee of $14.80 on $500 is about 2.96%.

Fraud insurance of $5 was also paid.
Payment fees are paid from the margin, along with shipping and ads.
**Subtract their total before any net-profit check.**
Ad cost per sale, break-even ROAS and break-even CPA
**Break-even ad spend per day** = number of sales needed × average order value (AOV, the average amount one customer spends).

Equivalent: sales needed per day = daily ad spend ÷ average order value.
Break-even cost per purchase = selling price − (product cost + shipping cost).

Example: a $39.90 product with a $17 fulfilment cost yields a margin of about $22.
Check: $39.90 − $17 = $22.90, so the source's $22 is rounded down.

**With $22.90, the break-even ROAS is 1.74, not 1.77.**
Break-even ROAS = selling price ÷ margin before ads.
Example: $39.90 ÷ $22 gives about 1.81 in the source's own $22 margin. $39.90 ÷ $22.90 gives 1.74. The source states 1.77.
**Ad campaigns must keep ROAS above break-even to make money.** Below it means a loss.
Break-even ROAS is the return on ad spend at which ad revenue only covers product cost and fees.
Break-even ROAS and CPA (continued)
Example: product cost $18 and selling price $39.99 give a break-even ROAS of **1.85** in the Dropship Toolkit (a tool).
Product cost alone gives $39.99 ÷ $21.99 = 1.82, so the 1.85 depends on the tool's fee assumptions.

If actual ROAS is above break-even, the product makes money.
If it is below, raise the price or choose a product with a lower cost of goods.

Break-even ROAS in the calculator = total revenue ÷ margin $.
Buy 1 gives $43 ÷ $32.50 = 1.32.

Buy 2, get 1 free gives $83 ÷ $60.30 = 1.38.
Target cost per acquisition (CPA) must be below break-even cost per purchase.

Example: a product sold at $30 that costs $10.
**Acquire each customer for under $20.** That difference is the margin available for advertising.

At the start, the margin of $20 is calculated without advertising expenses.
Other costs such as apps, Shopify and hiring are considered later.
**Once a product has run for more than a month, reserve about 5 to 10 percent** of product plus shipping cost for these.
For a store with several price points, calculate break-even ROAS from the lowest-priced product at the start.
**After about 100 orders, switch** to the actual average order value and the average cost of product plus shipping.
Work out break-even and selling price before setting the campaign structure (how you organize your ads).

Example: for a $40 product, the maximum CPA is around $15-$18.
Ad budget ceilings: keep ad cost per sale at or below 10% of MAP.

The 10% rule is a budget ceiling (a maximum) for net-profit planning.
Break-even CPA is the point where a sale stops making money.

These answer different questions, so check both.
Margin cushion: do not run a store with margins so thin that one day of ad account neglect could lose money.

Keep enough room in each product's margin to absorb mistakes and ad fluctuations (ups and downs in ad results).
Older advice (2021).
ROAS targets for paid launches
When launching a product on paid ads, start at a medium price point rather than a very cheap one.

**The minimum acceptable starting point is a 3.5x return on ad spend (ROAS).**
The long-term target is around 8x.

Raising average order value (AOV) can turn an unprofitable item into a profitable one.
The extra revenue covers the margin gap.
**Measure profitability per order after each AOV change.**
Gross versus net margin

Markup (the extra added on top of cost) to gross margin:
43% markup on wholesale gives about 30% gross profit.

54% markup on wholesale gives about 35% gross profit.
Gross margin per unit = selling price − supplier cost, before transaction fees, shipping and advertising.
Example: a product sold at $38.99 with a supplier cost of about $20 leaves roughly **$19 per unit** before those other costs.

Compare products by profit per order, and by how many orders the same total profit requires.
**Do not compare by margin percentage alone.**

A $50 product with $20 profit has a 40% margin.
A $3,000 product with $900 profit has only a 30% margin, but it earns **45 times more per sale**.

Older advice (2021-22).
A typical dropship net margin is about **30% of total sales revenue**.

Business margins: about **23%** after negotiating volume discounts with suppliers.
**A margin of 25% or higher is the target** for gross margin on products.

Products with thinner margins often cannot carry the cost of paid ads.
Older advice (2021).
Gross margin in the calculator:

Margin $ = Total Paid − Total Cost For Us.
Total Cost For Us = COGS + Pick N Pack (a fee per order for picking and packing) + Shipping + Gateway.

Margin % = Margin $ ÷ Total Paid.
The margin is therefore after product, fulfilment, shipping and gateway fees.
**It is before ad spend.**
The 70% profit margin threshold for slight price cuts below competitors does not say whether it is gross or net.
**Calculate it only after COGS and ad spend are subtracted,** so the number reflects what you actually keep.
Net margin
**Net profit margin after all costs must be at least 20%, and aim for 30%.**

Costs include cost of goods, shipping, ads, Shopify fees, merchant fees and other expenses.
Older advice (2021).

Target an average net profit margin of about **30%** across the business, after all costs.
Do not treat the MAP-to-wholesale spread alone as the margin.

Shipping and ads still need to be paid from it.
Net profit should aim for 30% of the sale.

A supplier that gives only about 15% margin leaves very little room for ad spend.
So reaching a 30% net profit target usually requires very low customer acquisition costs.
**Check this before you build a product list (catalogue) around that supplier.**

Target profit after shipping is about **25 to 30 percent** of the selling price, measured after freight.
Older advice (2023 is not flagged).

**A typical target margin is about $20 per product.**
Set the final price after you decide on bundles (several items sold together) and volume discounts, because these change the margin.
Choose products with a minimum margin of about $20.
Smaller margins make it harder to get sales. They also lead to more returns, complaints and chargebacks (payment disputes where the bank takes money back) as order volume grows.
When competitors charge close to the same price, **increase average order value through bundles** to improve profit.
Ratio example: a sourcing cost of about $20 and a selling price of about $40 was described as a very good ratio for a product.

**The wholesale cost should be about 50% of the selling price.** This is the typical target.
Lower margins make it difficult to pay for shipping and ads.
Older advice (2020).

A product with a 30% gross margin is thin. Review its pricing before scaling.
Thin-margin products leave little room for chargeback and refund costs.

**A product is only a winner if its profit margin is at least 18 to 25 percent.**
A product that loses money does not count as a winner, even if it sells.
Dollar and ratio tests (continued)

**Margin below 15%: reject the supplier.** Ad costs, shipping and payment processing fees must still be covered.
A healthy margin is needed on top of these costs.

Older advice (2019).
If wholesale includes shipping, or shipping is charged separately, the total landed cost still needs a margin around **30%, not 15%**.

Ad costs and processing fees must be paid from that margin.
Older advice (2019).
**Do not launch a store if most products have average margins of about 10 percent before ad costs.**

Negotiate better prices, or drop low-margin products from the store.
Older advice (2021).
Example: a store offered free shipping, a free gift and a price-match guarantee. Margins were too thin on about half its products.

Removing the price-match guarantee first restored margins, while keeping free shipping and the free gift.
Older advice (2021).

Returns: use a return rate of about **1% to 2% at most** for drop-shipped products.
If a supplier has no bad reviews, returns do not need to be built into product costs.

Older advice (2021).
**Reserve for returns:** list a reserve for returns among the costs per sale before setting any price.
Thin margins and low-margin suppliers are a problem at every scale. The margin rule applies to all products.

**Margin rule for shipping:** the minimum margin should be at least two to three times the shipping and fulfilment cost.
Small-margin products cannot absorb mistakes at scale.
**Keep margin for returns, complaints and chargebacks.**
With a MAP at 2x wholesale, the margin before expenses equals the wholesale cost (see the spread section).

**A product should leave a clear margin before you run any offer.**
Do not discount below the threshold.
Pricing from cost: setting the selling price
**Selling price** = total cost per order ÷ (1 − target margin).
Total cost per order means everything it costs you to deliver one order.
Total cost per order includes product cost, credit card fees, merchant account fees (bank charges for taking card payments), shipping and fulfilment cost per unit (the cost of packing

and sending each item).
For a **70%** margin, price = total cost ÷ 0.30.
Example: a product costs **$8** with a 70% margin target. Raise the price until margin reaches 70% after fees, shipping and fulfilment are added.
The sheet shows the selling price and margin. Check them against the **67-70%** range before you use the price.
Set the selling price so that **gross margin reaches 70%** of the price. Gross margin is the share of the price you keep after the costs of the order.
This 70% is the main pricing target for every product. If 70% is not reachable, **69%, 68% or 67%** is the acceptable minimum.
Gross margin on the calculator target applies to offers. Use the product-level benchmarks above when you screen products.
The two measure different bases. A product with product cost at **50%** of price will not reach 70% after fees.
Price the product at about **three times the wholesale cost** when it is not MAP-protected and still worth listing. MAP means the minimum advertised price, the lowest price the brand lets you show.
MAP-protected means the brand enforces that price. Wholesale cost is what the supplier charges you. Older advice (2019).
**Procedure: fix a product that shows no profit at MAP with flat-rate shipping** (flat-rate shipping means the same shipping price for every order) **
1. **Calculate** the profit per sale: selling price minus wholesale cost minus flat-rate shipping cost.
2. If the profit is zero or negative, **ask** the supplier's sales rep (the supplier's contact person for sales) whether a different price list applies to your account.
3. If no different price list exists and competitors sell at break-even (no gain, no loss), **do not list** the product.

4. If the product is still worth listing and is not MAP-protected, **price it at about three times the wholesale cost**. Do not run Google ads on it. Rely on organic sales (sales that come without paid ads).
Offers, bundles and discounts
**Check** that every offer makes financial sense.
The free item or gift must be affordable. The offer must still produce profit after ad spend (money spent on ads) and product costs.
An offer can never reduce the price to **zero**.
Each discount, free item or bonus must still cover product cost, shipping and ad spend. Calculate the margin before you run it.
A free gift only makes sense when its cost is low compared with the order value it is tied to.
Example of a cheap novelty product (a small, fun, low-cost item): sold at **$13**, with a supplier cost of $2 to $3 from AliExpress (a cheap online supplier marketplace).
This leaves roughly **$10** gross margin per unit before fees. The source judged this healthy for a low-return (few refunds), low-risk item.

Bundle costs: a necklace costs about $4-5 to make, a jewellery box about $1, and a three-item bundle about $13.
This gives a margin of about **$17** on a $29.90 price.
Bundles for buy-X-get-Y (buy some units, get others free): enter the **total** supplier cost of all units in the bundle.
Also enter the **total** price the customer pays, not per-unit figures. Mixing per-unit cost with bundle price distorts margin and break-even ROAS.
Break-even ROAS is the return on ad spend (sales per dollar of ads) at which ads just pay for themselves. ROAS stands for return on ad spend.
For a buy-X-get-Y offer, Price Before Discounts (the full price before any discount) must be the full price of every unit in the bundle, including the free units.

With a single unit at $40, Buy 2 get 1 free uses **$120** here.
An $80 Price On Site (the price the customer pays on your store) then shows a $40 saving and a Savings % of 33.33%.
**Enter** Price Before Discounts as the compare-at price (the higher, crossed-out price shown next to the sale price).
The sheet calculates Savings and Savings % from it. The savings then match the discount shoppers see on the product page.
Offers, bundles and discounts (continued)
To compare a bundle with a single unit, **divide** the bundle's Price On Site and its COGS (cost of goods sold, meaning total product cost) by all units in the bundle, including free ones.
For Buy 2 get 1 free at $80 price on site and $18 COGS across 3 units, this gives about **$26.67** revenue and $6.00 cost per unit. A single unit is $40.
Discount test example: Product B has $450 supplier shipping and free customer shipping.
Product B drops to $300 gross profit (12% gross margin) and $202.20 net profit (8.09% net margin) after fees. Gross profit is money left after product and direct costs.

Net profit is money left after all costs, including fees.
With a 5% discount, gross profit is $175. With 10%, $50. With **15%, −$75**. Older advice (2021-22).
New stores often do not sell at a profit at first. They may only break even.

The list price (the normal shelf price), supplier cost, negotiated supplier cost (a price agreed with the supplier), and whether shipping is charged to the customer are all adjustable levers (settings you can

change).
These levers take time to tune. Older advice (2021-22).
**Test** different price points and offer structures in the calculator before you launch them.
Each change moves margin, break-even ROAS and target CPA. Target CPA is the most you can spend on ads for one sale (CPA stands for cost per acquisition).

Comparing scenarios on paper shows which offer can still pay for ads.
Bundles raise average order value (AOV, the average amount spent per order).

This improves profit per order.
Discount-level spreadsheet: the build-phase product pricing sheet (the sheet made during store setup, with the tabs Product / Supplier Pricing).
It takes each product's list price, supplier cost and shipping paid by the customer. It shows gross profit and gross margin at **5%, 10% and 15%** off.

**Check** it before any discount to see how much margin each level leaves. Older advice (2021-22).
**Procedure: setting an offer for a new store with no sales history

1. **Compare** the MAP price of each product with its wholesale cost.
2. **Ask** the supplier for sample shipping costs.

3. **Calculate** the expected profit per sale from these numbers.
4. **Base the offer on that profit.** Do not choose a discount without these figures.
Margin calculators and sheets
**Calculator procedure (Margins & Offers sheet)**
1. **Make your own copy** of the shared margin calculator sheet (a spreadsheet for working out margins).
2. **List every offer** you run or plan to test, such as Buy 1, Buy 2 get 1 free or Buy 3 get 2 free. The list depends on your product.
3. **For each offer, enter the COGS** as the total supplier cost of all units the customer receives in that offer.
4. **Enter** the Pick N Pack cost (the fee for a company that picks and packs your orders) and the Shipping cost you pay. If shipping is already included in COGS, leave Shipping at 0.
5. **Check** that the Gateway column (the payment processing fee) uses your Shopify Payments rate (Shopify's own payment fee). The standard example is **5.5% of the price plus $0.30**.
6. **Enter Price On Site** as the total the customer pays for the offer, for example $80 for Buy 2 get 1 free.
7. If you charge shipping, **enter the Shipping Price** the customer pays.
8. **Read** Total Paid / Total Rev (the total money in from the customer), Margin $ (profit in dollars), Margin % (profit as a share of money in) and BE ROAS (break-even ROAS) for the offer.

9. **Enter Price Before Discounts** to see Savings and Savings %.
10. **Read Target CPA** for 2+ ROAS and for 2.5+ ROAS.
11. **Confirm** that Margin % is at least **70%**.

12. **Fill every cell** for each offer you run before you use its numbers.

The sheet's relationships, seen in both examples:

**Total Paid** = price on site + shipping charged.
**Margin $** = Total Paid − Total Cost For Us.
**Margin %** = Margin $ ÷ Total Paid.

**BE ROAS** = Total Paid ÷ Margin $.
**Target CPA** = Margin $ ÷ 2 for 2+ ROAS, and Margin $ ÷ 2.5 for 2.5+ ROAS.
Aim for a gross margin of at least **70%** on every offer before you run ads for it.
The 70% figure is the minimum target in this approach. An offer below it has little room for ad costs.
Shipping charged to the customer goes on the revenue side (Total Paid / Total Rev), not into the product price.
Shipping you pay for fulfilment goes in the Shipping column. It adds to total cost.
Mistake: **leaving a price or cost cell empty** makes the sheet show **#DIV/0!** (an error meaning "divided by zero").
This error appears in Margin %, BE ROAS, Savings % and Target CPA, because the formulas divide by zero.

It takes product cost and selling price and returns break-even ROAS.
Filtering products by net profit per sale
Start from the spread (the gap between two prices): MAP minus wholesale. Then **take out** shipping, fees and ads.
A product that does not leave enough after these is not a candidate.
Keep a product only if its net profit per sale (money left from one sale after all costs) is above roughly **10%**.
Products below this are not worth listing. Older advice (2019).
Net profit per sale check (target **30%** net, **20%** floor, where the floor is the lowest acceptable level): use the net-profit formula for each candidate.

Then compare against the threshold.
Compare candidates (products you are considering) by **profit per order**.
Also compare by how many orders the same total profit requires. Do not compare by margin % alone.
For a catalogue (your full list of products) with hundreds of products, **do not calculate every item**.
Focus on the best sellers. There are often fewer than 20 out of 500 products, and they give the highest leverage (the biggest effect on results).
For large catalogues, group products into price buckets (groups of similar prices), such as $2,000, $1,700, $1,500 and $1,300.

Use **averaged targets per bucket**. Older advice (2021-22).
Shipping-heavy items (products where shipping costs a lot) need the net check before listing. Margins can be very thin.
Amazon net check: profit before ads = sale price − wholesale − shipping − Amazon fees (the fees Amazon takes from each sale).
Products whose net profit is below the threshold, and that show no profit at MAP with flat-rate shipping: see the procedure above.
**Do not launch** a store on a supplier list where most products are around 10% margin before ads.
